chapter_theme: The decade of wishes (வேட்கைப் பத்து, marutham, Orampokiyar): in each poem the mother wishes long life and prosperity for the king Aadan Avini and his land, and the girl's side answers with wishes for the man of the field town, rising from his welfare and his house to an open suitor's chariot, marriage, his kept oath, freedom from gossip and the bride taken to his town (1-10).

1.reading: The speaker reports that the mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, abundant paddy and great gold, while she and her companion wished that the man of the thriving town, where the kaanji is in bud and the small fish are full of roe, may live long, and his bard with him.
1.nuance: The decade's frame is set here: one line of the mother's wishes for the king and the land, one line of 'we' wishing for the lover, so a private love is set inside a public prayer for the realm. Wishing the bard well too places the lover among the bards who carry his messages and his fame. The budding tree and the fish heavy with roe are read by some as a promise of a fruitful house, but the poem itself draws no match, so they stay scene.

thinai_evidence.note: budding kaanji, roe-filled fish and the lord of a watered town are things of the field country

2.reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that the fields may yield and alms-seekers may come, while the speaker and her companion wished that their bond with the man of the cool ford, where the neythal rivals the many-petalled blue lily, may grow from generation to generation.
2.nuance: The mother's wish that suppliants come is a king's virtue, giving; the girls' wish answers it with a bond that lasts 'line after line' (வழிவழி), a marriage that outlives the lovers. The two lilies matching each other at the ford sit beside the wish for a lasting bond as an image of a well-matched pair, though the poem does not say so.

thinai_evidence.note: water lilies at the cool ford of a town fix the field country

comparisons.tenor: the neythal lily at the ford

3.reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that milk may flow and the bulls thrive, while the speaker and her companion wished that the household of the man of the flower-crowded town, where the ploughmen who sowed go home with their paddy, may flourish.
3.nuance: The wish is for his மனை வாழ்க்கை, the life of a house, which the girls can only share if he marries: so the blessing is also a claim. The ploughmen who sowed and now carry home the grain fit that claim (what was begun is brought home), but the poem leaves the match unspoken.

thinai_evidence.note: ploughmen returning with the harvest are the labour of the field country

4.reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that his enemies be reduced to eating grass and the brahmins chant their learning, while the speaker and her companion wished that the chest of the man of the field town, where sugarcane flowers and paddy bears grain, may never become a common pond.
4.nuance: பழனம் is the town's shared water and field, open to all; to wish that his chest not become one is to fear in advance the straying husband of the field country, whose embrace every woman of the town might use. The mother's wish that enemies be brought to grass and the girls' wish against a shared chest both ask that something stay in its rightful place.

thinai_evidence.note: flowering cane, grain-bearing paddy and the wet field are things of the field country

5.reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that there be no hunger and disease go far away, while the speaker and her companion wished that the chariot of the man of the cool ford, where the male crocodile swallows fish whole, may stand at their front gate.
5.nuance: A chariot standing openly at the front gate is the sign of a man who comes as a suitor by day, not a secret lover by night, so the wish asks for marriage without naming it. The male crocodile gulping whole fish is sometimes read as a warning about a greedy lover, but nothing in the poem matches it to him, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the crocodile and fish of the town's ford are things of the field country

6.reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that the king's wars cease and his years increase, while the speaker and her companion wished that the man of the cool ford, where lotus buds rise in a pond already in flower, may marry her and that their father may give her to him.
6.nuance: This is the decade's plainest wish: வரைக, let him marry, and எந்தையும் கொடுக்க, let our father give, naming both halves of the rite. The 'our father' (எந்தை) shows the speaker speaks as one with the girl. The pond in flower with lotuses still in bud sets a scene of ripeness about to open.

thinai_evidence.note: the lotus pond at the town's ford is of the field country

7.reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that virtue flourish greatly and all else perish, while the speaker and her companion wished that the man of the cool ford, where a heron sits with its kin in the tufted-flowered marutham tree, may take her and go to his own town.
7.nuance: To be taken to his town is the bride's departure from her father's house; the heron settled among its kin (கிளை) in the tree of the field country shows what she is to have there, a place in his kindred.

thinai_evidence.note: the marutham tree and the heron of the ford are things of the field country

iraicchi.act: the heron dwells with its kin in the marutham tree
iraicchi.sense: as the heron lives among its own flock, the man should bring her to live among his kin in his own town

8.reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that he rule justly and there be no theft, while the speaker and her companion wished that the oath sworn here by the man of the flower-crowded town, where a lovely peacock sits on the swaying bough of a mango, may come true.
8.nuance: சூள் இவண் is 'the oath here': the vow was sworn in this place, to the girl, and the wish is that it 'prove true' (வாய்ப்பதாக), which admits it might not. The mother's wish against theft (களவு இல் ஆகுக) uses the same word as hidden love, களவு, so the decade's two wish-lines touch: let there be no stealing in the land, and let the lover's stolen union be made good by his word.

thinai_evidence.note: the mango in a town of many flowers sets the field country; the peacock is a hill bird out of place

9.reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that good increase greatly and harm vanish, while the speaker and her companion wished that their bond with the man of the cool ford, where the heron that has fed on kayal fish sleeps on the straw stacks, may not become the talk of the town.
9.nuance: அம்பல் is the first low murmur of gossip, before it becomes open அலர்; the wish is that the secret bond be settled before the town can name it. The heron that has eaten its fill and sleeps on the stack in plain view of the field may hint at a love that should not be left lying in the open, but the poem draws no match, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the heron and the threshed straw stacks of the ford town are of the field country

10.reading: The mother wished long life to Aadan Avini, that the rains come in season and wealth greatly increase, while the speaker and her companion wished that the man of the cool ford, where small fish smelling of flesh lie under the flowering mango, may take her with him and go.
10.nuance: The decade closes as poem 7 did, with the wish that he take her and go (கொண்டனன் செல்க), but here 'with him' (தன்னோடு) replaces 'to his town': the last wish is simply to be with him. The mother's wish for timely rain is the oldest of a king's blessings.

thinai_evidence.note: the mango by the water and the small fish of the ford fix the field country

links.note: Ainkurunuru 4: the girls wish that the lover's chest never become a common pond (பழனம்). Kural 1311: the wife refuses her husband's chest because all women feast on it in common with their eyes.
links.teaches: The fear the Ainkurunuru girls voice before marriage, that his chest may become common property, is the very charge the Kural's wife brings in a sulk after it, so the two show the marutham husband's straying anticipated as a danger and then turned into a reason to refuse him.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 9: the girls wish that their bond with the lover not become town gossip (அம்பல்). Kural 1143: the man welcomes the gossip the whole town knows, since it feels like having her already.
links.teaches: The same talk of the town that the women pray to escape is a pleasure the man savours, so read together the two show that in secret love gossip threatened the woman's standing while it flattered the man's hopes.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 8: the mother wishes that the king rule justly and there be no theft (and in poem 10, that the rains come). Kural 545: rain and harvest gather in the land of a king who rules by the sceptre's nature.
links.teaches: The mother's prayers for just rule and for timely rain stand as separate wishes in the decade, while the Kural makes the second follow from the first, so a household's prayer list shows the belief that the Kural later states as a law of kingship.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 8: the girls wish that the lover's oath sworn here may prove true. Kuruntokai 53: the friend tells the man of the fields that what afflicts them is the oath he swore at the broad ford of their town, holding the girl's forearm.
links.teaches: The oath the Ainkurunuru girls hope will come true is, in the Kuruntokai, already the cause of their suffering, so the pair shows the kalavu vow of the field country both as the girl's only security and as the wound when it lags.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 5: the girls wish that the lover's chariot stand at their front gate. Akananuru 160: the friend tells the girl that his chariot, which used to come by night, has now come by day, loudly, for the whole village to see.
links.teaches: The Akananuru scene shows what the Ainkurunuru wish means: a chariot that comes by day to the gate, seen by the village, is a suitor's public claim, so the single wish for 'the chariot at our gate' is a request for marriage.

links.note: Ainkurunuru 6: may he marry her and our father give her. Ainkurunuru 7: may he take her and go to his own town.
links.teaches: Read in order, the decade's wishes walk through the rite step by step, the father's giving (6) and then the bride's leaving for the husband's town (7), so the series records the sequence of a Sangam marriage that no single poem states.

new_concepts.gloss: a blessing or wish spoken for another's welfare, the frame of a whole decade of the Ainkurunuru

source_issues: 1-10: the colophon has no thurai for this decade and the e-text prints no decade title; the speaker (thozhi, speaking with the girl as 'we', யாமே) and addressee are inferred from the poems, so occasion words are null.
9 line 1: ஆதன்வாழி is printed without the space found in line 1 of the other nine poems.
